To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) propranolol binds stronger to Amberlite™ than does potassium and that (2) the heat effect is continuous and non-linear with the degree of loading of propranololic acid.

the exchange capacity and affinity of Amberlite™ is higher for propranolol than for potassium and that the heat effects of the binding of propanolol to Amberlite™ change continuously with the degree of loading.

the ion exchange of propranolola H + ions with Amberlite™ is more favorable than the exchange of K + ions, and that the heat effects of ion exchange of propanolol- H + are continuously changing with the degree of loading, while those of potassium are constant.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel, simple and rapid method to determine the equilibrium concentrations and amount of drug bound to the resin in a model system of propranololaHCl/Amberlite™, and to compare it with the system KCl/Amberlita™.
the characterization of the ion exchange process between the protonated form of the drug propranolol and Amberlite™ IRP 69 resin by isothermal calorimet- ric and spectroscopic measurements.
the characterization of the ion ex- change reaction between propranolol-H + /K + and Amberlite™ by both, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and (flame) photometric equilibrium analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the binding of pro- pranolol-H + to the ion ex- change resin is a more complex process than that of the potassium ions.
, in contrast to the potassium system, in the propranolol system the ion exchange is accompanied by a continuous variation of the specific heat effect.
the exchange of potassium with propranololidium ions is a two-step process, while that of propranololidi- um with potassium is a single-step process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the exchange of propranol- ol- H + by K + from the resin is an enthalpy-driven, entropy-disfavoured process.
propranolol is bound more tightly to the ion exchange resin Amberlite™ than potassium.

the ion exchange reaction between the cationic drug propranolol-H + and Amberlite™ IRP 69 resin is more complex than the reaction between K + and the resin, and that the ion exchange of propranol- ol-H + is accompanied by specific heat effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to measure the heat of reaction between a drug and an ion exchange resin, and that the heat of reaction is not a constant, but depends on the degree of loading.
the affinity of Amberlite™ towards propranolol is higher than towards potassium.
it is not possible to predict the heat effect of an ion exchange reaction based on the stoichiometry of the ion exchanger and the ions involved.
